props.title: Some Girls Do

sections.content: Some Girls Do (1969) fits into the fascinating wave of 1960s spy spoofs that followed the James Bond phenomenon. This Richard Johnson vehicle, a sequel to Bulldog Drummond Deadlier Than the Female (1967), embraces the campy tech-obsessed espionage trends of its era. Like Casino Royale (1967) and Our Man Flint (1966), it plays with genre tropes through a lens of swinging sixties style - beautiful robot women, outlandish gadgets, and tongue-in-cheek humor define the film's approach.

sections.content: The film's plot about robot women assassins taps into contemporary anxieties about technology and automation, similar to Dr. Goldfoot and the Girl Bombs (1966) and Dr. Goldfoot and the Bikini Machine (1965). Director Robert Miller embraces the absurdity while maintaining just enough spy thriller elements to keep the action moving. The film particularly shines in its elaborate set pieces and production design that capture the mod aesthetic of late 60s British cinema.

Beyond its surface charms, Some Girls Do represents a key moment in British cinema's relationship with American spy films. While James Bond maintained a relatively serious tone in You Only Live Twice (1967), these smaller productions allowed for more playful deconstruction of spy movie conventions. The film shares DNA with other British spy spoofs like Hot Enough for June (1964) and Where the Spies Are (1966). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Spy Spoofs

movies.title: Dr. Goldfoot and the Bikini Machine
movies.slug: Vincent Price stars as a mad scientist creating robot women in this spy comedy

sections.content: The late 1960s marked peak saturation for spy spoofs, with Some Girls Do arriving just as the genre began to wear thin. Films like In Like Flint (1967) and Modesty Blaise (1966) had already pushed the formula to its limits. What makes Some Girls Do interesting is how it straddles the line between legitimate thriller and outright parody, something later films like Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery (1997) would reference.
